question: A 30-year-old man comes to the physician because of an episode of bloody vomiting this morning and a 1-week history of burning upper abdominal pain. Two weeks ago, he sustained a head injury and was in a coma for 3 days. An endoscopy shows multiple, shallow hemorrhagic lesions predominantly in the gastric fundus and greater curvature. Biopsies show patchy loss of epithelium and an acute inflammatory infiltrate in the lamina propria that does not extend beyond the muscularis mucosa. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
analysis: The patient's history of a recent head injury and subsequent coma, followed by symptoms of bloody vomiting and upper abdominal pain, suggests a stress-related mucosal disease. The endoscopic findings of multiple, shallow hemorrhagic lesions predominantly in the gastric fundus and greater curvature, along with the histological findings of patchy loss of epithelium and acute inflammatory infiltrate confined to the lamina propria, are characteristic of Cushing ulcer. Cushing ulcers are stress ulcers associated with increased intracranial pressure or brain injury, leading to increased gastric acid production mediated by vagal stimulation.
